again.e: From Middle English agayn, from Old English onġēan (“against, again”), from Proto-West Germanic *in gagin, from Proto-Germanic *in gagin. By surface analysis, on- + gain (“against”).
again.g: Another time: indicating a repeat of an action.

against.e: Formed from Middle English ayenes, agenes, againes (“in opposition to”), a southern variant of agen, or directly from again, either way with adverbial genitive singular ending -es; the parasitic -t was added circa 1350, probably by confusion with the superlative ending -est. By surface analysis, again + -st (excrescent ending).

agate.e: From Middle French agathe, from Latin achatēs, from Ancient Greek ἀχάτης (akhátēs, “agate”).
agate.g: A semitransparent, uncrystallized silicate mineral and semiprecious stone, presenting various tints in the same specimen, with colors delica

agate.e: From Late Middle English agate, a gate. Equivalent to a- (“on”) + gate (“way, path”).

age.e: From Middle English age, Old French aage, eage, edage, from an assumed Vulgar Latin *aetāticum, derived from Latin aetātem, itself derived from aevum (“lifetime”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyu- (“vital force”). Originally found mostly as a participial adjective, probably an adjective in -ed, derived from the noun, reanalyzed to create a verb.
age.g: The amount of time that some being has been alive, or that some thing has been in existence, as measured from its birth or origin until the

agent.e: From Latin agēns, present active participle of agere (“to drive, lead, conduct, manage, perform, do”).
agent.g: One who exerts power, or has the power to act.

aggravate.e: Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English. By surface analysis, ag- + grave (“heavy”) + -ate (“verb suffix”).
aggravate.g: To make (an offence) worse or more severe; to increase in offensiveness or heinousness.

aggravation.g: The act of aggravating, or making worse; used of evils, natural or moral; the act of increasing in severity or heinousness; something additi

aggressor.g: The person or country that first attacks or makes an aggression; that begins hostility or a quarrel; an assailant.

aging.g: The process of becoming older or more mature.

agitate.e: From Middle English agitat(e) (“set in motion”), borrowed from Latin agitātus, perfect passive participle of agitō (“to put in motion”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), frequentative of agō (“to drive, move, push”), see -tō.
agitate.g: To disturb or excite; to perturb or stir up (a person).

ago.e: From Middle English ago, agon (“passed”), past participle of agon (“to depart, escape, pass”), from Old English āgān (“to go away, pass away, go forth, come to pass”), from Proto-Germanic *uz- (“out”), *gāną (“to go”), equivalent to a- + gone, and by surface analysis, a- + go.
ago.g: Before now, before the present time

agony.e: 14th century, via Old French and Latin from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía, “emulation, competition, struggle”), from ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”). Specifically of the struggle that precedes death (mortal agony) from the 1540s. By surface analysis, agon + -y. The sense of "extreme pain" from c. 1600.

agree.e: From Middle English agreen, from Old French agreer (“to accept or receive kindly”), from a gré (“favorably”), from Latin ad (“to”) + gratum (“pleasing”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“to welcome, greet, praise”).
agree.g: To be in harmony about an opinion, statement, or action; to have a consistent idea between two or more people.

agreement.e: From Middle English agrement, agreement, from Old French agrement, agreement. Morphologically agree + -ment.
agreement.g: An understanding between entities to follow a specific course of conduct.

aground.e: From Middle English agrounde, on grounde (“on ground”), equivalent to a- + ground.

ague.e: From Middle English agu, ague, borrowed from Middle French (fievre) aguë, “acute (fever)” (Modern French fièvre aiguë), from Late Latin (febris) acuta (“acute fever”), from Latin acūtus (“sharp, acute”) + febris (“fever”).
